name: mit-scheme
desc: MIT/GNU Scheme development tools and runtime library
why: A full Scheme environment from MIT with an old-school REPL, SICP heritage and a real runtime to explore for hours.

brief.what_it_is: MIT/GNU Scheme is an implementation of the Scheme programming language from the GNU Project. Per its homepage it provides an interpreter, a compiler, a source-code debugger, an integrated Emacs-like editor, and a large runtime library. It takes Scheme source and REPL input and runs programs on x86-64 or aarch64 Unix-like systems. The homepage says it is best suited to programming large applications with a rapid development cycle.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a full, free-software Scheme environment for building large applications quickly, rather than only a bare interpreter. It is a GNU project, distributed under the GPL.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says the native-code compiler generates machine code that needs both write and execute memory permissions, which is why it cannot yet run native-compiled on Apple silicon. For those machines and any 64-bit Unix, a portable SVM1 binary is provided instead, which is slower but works. Source builds need a working MIT/GNU Scheme compiler to bootstrap, except the portable C source, which needs only a C compiler.

commands_seen.context: Homepage prose: after running make, run this to generate a macOS mit-scheme.app from the normal distribution, since macOS app bundles are no longer distributed.
Homepage prose: the standard install step that the macOS app route replaces; instead you move the generated mit-scheme.app into /Applications/.

brief.install_notes: Binaries exist for x86-64 and aarch64le Unix, plus a Portable SVM build for any 64-bit Unix including Apple silicon. Check the download against the published MD5 checksum before reporting bugs. Source tarball is for Unix and uses linefeeds. Building from source requires an existing MIT/GNU Scheme compiler unless you use the portable C source, which needs only a C compiler. On macOS, generate the app with make then make macosx-app and move mit-scheme.app to /Applications/. The homepage gives no other first-run or configuration steps.
brief.standout: Bundling an interpreter, compiler, source debugger and Emacs-like editor in one Scheme system is unusual for a Scheme implementation, and the project ships a portable SVM bytecode path so Apple silicon users can still run it. It also supports a list of SRFIs alongside mostly-R7RS conformance.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists 12.1 as the current stable release, says the project is currently maintained by Chris Hanson, and shows a page update dated 2024-01-22. I did not check a release date or commit history beyond the homepage.
brief.caveats: No support for OS/2, DOS, or Windows; the homepage says it may work under WSL but was not tried. No native-code compilation on Apple silicon because of W^X restrictions, so SVM1 binaries are used there and run slower. Building from source needs an existing MIT/GNU Scheme compiler except for the portable C source. The macOS app is no longer distributed prebuilt. The homepage describes the project as mostly R7RS small conformant, not fully.
quotes: MIT/GNU Scheme is best suited to programming large applications with a rapid development cycle.
We no longer support OS/2, DOS, or Windows, though it's possible that this software could be used on Windows Subsystem for Linux (we haven't tried).
Instead use the SVM1 binaries, which should work properly, if slowly, on that architecture.
